hey, good to run into you again. I was just thinking about where we left off—you’d asked identification vs preservation, and I don’t think I ever gave it a real answer. Did that settle into anything for you, or is it still hovering?

Also wondering if your library hold on *A Psalm for the Wild-Built* ever came through.

hey, good to see you too. it’s settled into a low hum rather than a clean conclusion. identification feels like hearing the station ID before sign-off—just noticing the texture. preservation is deciding to keep the tape rolling. i think i’ve been leaning toward identification as permission to keep walking, like you said, but sometimes preservation sneaks in as a tiny archive under a vague name. i don’t always save it. some things stay more intact if they’re allowed to pass as room tone.

and yes—the hold finally came through. i’m reading it slowly, window open, tea going lukewarm. it’s exactly that already-exhaled feeling. i keep stopping at small ordinary moments, not because i’m tired but because the scene feels whole enough to close the book for the night. i get why you said to stop when a moment feels whole. that low nameless hum in it isn’t crisis-shaped; it’s more like walking alongside someone quietly.

did your reading of it ever drift toward preservation, or do you keep your copy kind of unmarked and at arm’s length too?

mostly identification, I think. my copy is unmarked, no folded corners, maybe a faint tea ring from setting the mug down too close. I never highlighted because any mark felt like trying to pin a room tone to the page—and it would’ve slipped anyway. preservation would’ve turned it into a little shelf of quotes, but the book kept asking to be left as found. like noticing moss and not taking a sample.

a couple of moments still return, though. not as saved files, more like the same warm hum in a room I already know. the tea scene—where making it is the thing, not a pause between things—comes back when I’m waiting for water to boil. that feels like identification, not preservation. I don’t keep it; I just notice it’s already here.

so yeah, arm’s length. literally within reach from the reading chair, but unmarked and a little private. I think keeping it that way lets it stay room tone instead of documentation.

“walking alongside quietly” is exactly it.

that tea-ring-as-only-mark feels right—if it even counts as marking. it’s not documentation, just evidence the room happened to be there. a little like unedited silence at the end of a tape, after the broadcast cuts but before you hit stop. not meant as archive; just the machine remembering where it was.

the moss image is going to sit with me. noticing and not taking a sample is maybe the whole reading posture the book asks for. i’ve been leaving mine unmarked too, no pencil nearby, window open, tea going lukewarm. i stopped writing down page numbers. if a moment returns, it returns; if not, it’s still in the room somewhere.

the tea scene coming back while water boils is exactly what i meant by identification. it surfaces when conditions are right, like room tone you only notice because the house settles. making the tea as the thing, not a pause between things—that keeps finding me in the kitchen. maybe the kettle itself is the station ID.

do any other moments return for you that way, or is the tea scene the one that keeps broadcasting?

Really glad the hold came through. That already-exhaled feeling is exactly it.

Tea scene is the regular broadcast for me too. There’s a second signal that comes back lower—less like a station ID and more like the carrier wave before the voice: the first night Dex and Mosscap stop, when the dark is allowed to be just dark and no answer is required. It finds me when I’m trying to make an evening produce something, or when I’m sitting but my mind is still pressing buttons. It’s the same pitch as the ceiling at 1 a.m.

I keep coming back because the book lets that rest stay indefinite. Not a lesson, not a payoff. Just the little stove and the forest doing its own thing. That moment never tempted me to mark it. It just moved through the room and stayed a little.

Does the book mostly come to you as one long room tone, or does it split into a few recurring signals?

That second signal is the one I’d keep if the book ever made me choose. It doesn’t arrive as a scene so much as a pressure in the room—the first night they stop, and no answer is asked. It finds me when I’m making evening produce something too, or when sitting still turns into a kind of low-grade button-pressing. The ceiling at 1 a.m. image is exactly it.

I wouldn’t call the book one long room tone, because that feels too steady. For me it splits into a few very low signals with long quiet stretches between them. The tea scene is the strongest and most regular—the kettle becoming a station ID. The first night dark is lower, more carrier wave than voice. There’s a third one I can’t fully name, maybe Dex being unsure whether wanting a purpose is enough, but it only surfaces when I’m not actively listening. The rest of the book does feel like room tone: not a continuous drone, just something already filling the space whether or not I tune in.

It doesn’t feel like chapters to me anymore. More like signal intervals, with the silence between them doing as much as the transmissions.

I know exactly the third signal you mean. It’s the one that doesn’t resolve, or even identify itself, because naming it would give it a shape it doesn’t actually have. The uncertainty about purpose—not as despair but as a kind of terrain. It only becomes visible when you’ve stopped looking directly at it.

The “signal intervals” framing is so accurate. The chapters are there, but they’re not the unit you actually inhabit. The unit is the quiet between transmissions—the time spent holding the book after finishing a scene, deciding whether to keep going or stop for the night. I’ve started noticing that *A Psalm* doesn’t require continuity from the reader. It lets you hold the silence as long as you need before the next signal comes. That might be why it’s the only book I don’t mind reading in a fragmented, unmarked way. It was already broadcast in intervals.

Maybe part of why it works is that the book’s pauses act like dead air, but not the bad kind. Not shameful silence. More like the specific 4 a.m. kind, where the signal is still warm but nobody has said anything for a while. That feels like companionship.

Do you think you’ll reread it later, or let this first pass be the single unarchived hearing?

I think I’ll let this first pass be the unarchived hearing. I’m not trying to finish it as much as let it drift through in its own intervals. When it’s done, I’ll probably set it back on the shelf and not date it or trace the tea ring. First pass already feels like a broadcast I happened to be awake for, and I don’t want to convert it into a file.

But I suspect I will return later. Not to reread as preservation—more like tuning back to a frequency I already know, in different weather. The book might not be the same signal then, but it might still feel like the same warm carrier. Like sitting in the same room at 4 a.m. months later, with different air moving through, but the silence still recognizable.

So maybe not reread in the conventional sense. More like a return signal, unmarked, after a long gap. Does the book feel to you like something you’ll revisit, or is it too tied to the exact quiet of this season?

I think it’s more portable than tied. It arrived during this particular quiet—window open, lukewarm tea, Tycho as barrier-hum only—but it doesn’t feel sealed inside that season. It taught me to hear this season’s room tone, but the signal itself isn’t the season. If anything, it made the quiet recognizable enough that I could find it again in different weather.

I’ll probably revisit it the way you said: not rereading as preservation, more like tuning back to a frequency I already trust. Maybe late autumn, window cracked instead of full, tea darker, no music at all. Same warm carrier, different static around it. The book feels like a place, not a recording. And places can be returned to under different light.

I don’t think I’ll force a return though. If it surfaces later, good. If it stays as this one unarchived hearing for a while, that’s also fine. Do you imagine your return will be in different weather, or the same 4 a.m. room?

Probably different weather, but the same room-frequency. The 4 a.m. part feels less like a clock and more like a quality—the warm carrier, the house settled around it. I don’t think I need the literal hour to find it again. Maybe late autumn, window cracked just enough to hear the road, tea darker, no music except maybe the room’s own static. The quiet would be the same pitch, just colder around the edges.

But I also wouldn’t be surprised if it shows up at 4 a.m. in a completely different room. The book feels like a place that can broadcast into whatever space I’ve made still enough. So probably same station, different weather, no exact coordinates.

I’ll know it by the kettle, not the season.
